metadata.title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study analyzed PISA 2022 mathematics data for the United States and merged student and school files using the school ID (CNTSCHID), assigning school-level predictors to students within the same school. The analytic sample comprised 4,552 students in 154 schools, with grade distribution across 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, and 12th grades. Although the authors note that PISA provides complex, multistage clustered sampling and that sampling weights can be important in traditional regression, they explicitly did not include sampling weights in the ML analyses. This omission is justified by the authors as an ML-specific choice (tree-based ensembles) and is a limitation because hierarchical clustering and unequal selection probabilities are not fully accounted for via survey weighting.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 mathematics assessment data for 15-year-old students in the United States. Merged student and school questionnaires using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were attached to students in the same school. For preprocessing, removed predictors with >50% missing values; removed identical predictors (same values for all students); removed redundant predictors to reduce collinearity (e.g., retained ESCS and excluded the component DVs used to compute it). Imputed remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation). Split the cleaned dataset into training (80%, N=3,644) and test (20%, N=908) sets; model training and evaluation were repeated for each of the 10 math plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison for reduced predictor sets: Random Forest (rMSE=69.82; 5 predictors; training time=129.27 s), XGBoost (rMSE=66.39; 10 predictors; training time=4.14 s), LightGBM (rMSE=66.36; 10 predictors; training time=22.93 s). Best model by combined accuracy and efficiency: XGBoost with rMSE=66.39 and training time=4.14 s.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for U.S. 15-year-olds, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-learning to predict mathematics achievement (PVs), finding that XGBoost achieved lower prediction error than Random Forest and slightly lower error than LightGBM while also being substantially faster. This indicates that data-driven, tree-based ensemble models can identify a compact set of actionable student and home-context predictors for U.S. math performance, supporting targeted interventions focused on self-efficacy and foundational math familiarity, though the study does not apply sampling weights and thus results may not fully reflect population-representative uncertainty.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2022 mathematics data for the United States (4,552 students in 154 schools; grades 8–12) and predicted mathematics achievement using all 10 math plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH). After cleaning predictors (dropping >50% missing predictors, removing identical/redundant variables) and imputing remaining missing values with missForest, the authors trained three ensemble tree models—Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—using 5-fold cross-validation on an 80/20 train/test split. For reduced models using ML-selected predictors, XGBoost produced rMSE=66.39 with training time=4.14 s, outperforming Random Forest (rMSE=69.82; 129.27 s) and matching LightGBM’s accuracy (rMSE=66.36; 22.93 s) while being much more efficient. The most influential predictors included mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-directed learning. A key limitation is that sampling weights were not used in the ML models, and the interpretability relies on ALE plots (predictive associations, not causal effects).
